justification: Fresh read against the current top-ranking pages for "tcp vs udp" confirms round 1's finding still holds: GeeksforGeeks is a definitional comparison table with no code, no diagrams and no RFC citations, and Guru99 is a beginner tutorial with two decorative comparison images, no code, no packet or handshake detail, and no primary sourcing. This article clears both by a wide margin: six independent runnable loopback programs (UDP datagram-boundary echo, a deliberately dumb TCP echo that coalesces three writes, length-prefixed framing, a TCP flow-control stall against a sleeping receiver, a UDP send-storm against a shrunk receive buffer, and a connected-UDP ICMP-unreachable demo), three original diagrams, and inline RFC citations. I re-verified sourcing myself rather than trusting round 1's spot-check: RFC 9293 section 2.2 and 3.7 quotes are verbatim; the new RFC 5681 section 3/3.1 quotes this round is specifically asked to check (slow start's "at most SMSS bytes... for each ACK," congestion avoidance's "roughly 1 full-sized segment per round-trip time," and "using loss as the signal of congestion") are all verbatim and correctly attributed; RFC 8085 section 1's congestion-control requirement and the TFRC/one-datagram-per-RTT recommendations in 3.1.2/3.1.3 are accurately paraphrased and cited; RFC 792's "may send a destination unreachable message" is verbatim. Both round-1 findings are genuinely fixed, not just touched: the toolchain sentence now sits after the tcp-window code and output block, immediately before the interpretation of the 560-write/2.3 MB stall, matching the placement pattern in the published sibling how-the-internet-works.md ("Measurements from here on were taken on..." placed right after the first real per-machine numbers, not in the opening paragraph); and the payment exercise no longer claims TCP gives exactly-once delivery, instead stating plainly that a timeout-then-retry can double-submit and that exactly-once needs an idempotency key at the application layer, which matches the fix the round-1 review asked for. I attempted a distinctive-sentence copy check via search (budget-limited to a handful of queries plus a CAPTCHA wall on DuckDuckGo); the phrases I could test against Bing returned no matches to any other source, and nothing in the piece reads as paraphrased from the compared pages, whose coverage is too shallow to paraphrase from anyway. The one new issue this round is a same-pillar near-duplicate risk, not present in round 1's findings: this article's three-way-handshake sentence ("the initiator sends a segment with the SYN flag... the responder answers with its own SYN, plus an acknowledgment... the initiator acknowledges that in turn") mirrors the published sibling's handshake sentence clause-for-clause ("The client sends a segment with the SYN flag... the server answers with its own SYN and an acknowledgment... the client acknowledges that"), differing only by swapping client/server for initiator/responder. Both cite the same RFC 9293 section 3.5, but the identical three-clause architecture across two pillar siblings reads as one being drafted against the other as a template rather than independently from the RFC. That keeps this at "equal to the best reference quality with only nits" rather than a clean pass on originality grounds, so the score moves up from round 1's 8.4 (which was capped by a real major plus a real minor) but stays a shade under 8.5.

issues.problem: This sentence's three-clause structure (side A sends SYN + starting sequence number; side B answers with its own SYN plus an ack; side A acks that) matches, clause for clause, the handshake sentence in the published sibling article `networking/how-the-internet-works.md` ("What ConnectAsync did" section), differing only in using initiator/responder instead of client/server. Both cite the same RFC 9293 section 3.5. Two sibling pages in the same pillar describing the same mechanism in near-identical sentence architecture is the kind of same-pillar near-duplication an AdSense/quality reviewer flags, even though neither passage is copied from an outside source.
